HOA ASSESSMENT LIEN AND FORECLOSURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA · Pat T. Alvarez

HOA ASSESSMENT LIEN AND FORECLOSURE — INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes, in general terms, the statutory lien and foreclosure process available to a homeowners association under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, Civil Code §§ 5650–5740, for unpaid assessments owed by an owner of a separate interest. It concerns the separate interest commonly known as 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA, owned of record by Pat T. Alvarez, and assessments and related charges owed to Meadowbrook Homeowners Association. This process is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Davis-Stirling Act's disclosure article (Civil Code § 4525 et seq.), and distinct from a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure of a deed of trust under Civil Code §§ 2924 et seq. Here, the creditor is the association itself, collecting a debt for unpaid regular or special assessments — not a mortgage lender collecting a loan secured by a deed of trust. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien; it does not initiate, accelerate, halt, postpone, or complete any collection or foreclosure action; and it does not determine whether any specific assessment, fine, fee, or other charge is validly owed by Pat T. Alvarez, or whether any actual notice, recording, board vote, or sale relating to this property has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

THE ASSESSMENT DEBT AND WHEN IT BECOMES DELINQUENT
Under California Civil Code § 5650(a), "[a] regular or special assessment and any late charges, reasonable fees and costs of collection, reasonable attorney’s fees, if any, and interest, if any, as determined in accordance with subdivision (b), shall be a debt of the owner of the separate interest at the time the assessment or other sums are levied." Section 5650(b) fixes when that debt becomes delinquent and what may then be added to it: regular and special assessments are "delinquent 15 days after they become due, unless the declaration provides a longer time period," and once delinquent the association may recover reasonable costs of collection (including reasonable attorney's fees), "a late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars ($10), whichever is greater" (unless the declaration sets a smaller amount), and interest "at an annual interest rate not to exceed 12 percent, commencing 30 days after the assessment becomes due" (unless the declaration sets a lower rate). If a dollar figure has been stated as delinquent on Pat T. Alvarez's account with Meadowbrook Homeowners Association, it is stated as: $2,450.00, as of March 1, 2026.

  Known gap: Civil Code § 5650 creates the underlying personal debt owed by the owner and fixes the 15-day delinquency trigger and the statutory caps on late charges (10% or $10, whichever is greater) and interest (12% per annum); it does not itself create a recorded lien on the owner's separate interest — that additional step is governed by a separate statute, Civil Code § 5675, addressed in another clause of this document. The two citations in this clause are to subsections (a) and (b) of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 5650; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

PRE-LIEN NOTICE — 30 DAYS' WRITTEN NOTICE BEFORE RECORDING A LIEN
Before recording a lien for delinquent assessments against 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA to collect a debt owed by Pat T. Alvarez, California law requires the association to give written notice and certain rights. Civil Code § 5660 provides: "At least 30 days prior to recording a lien upon the separate interest of the owner of record to collect a debt that is past due under Section 5650, the association shall notify the owner of record in writing by certified mail" of a specified list of items. Under § 5660(a), those items include "a general description of the collection and lien enforcement procedures of the association," the owner's right to inspect association records, and a required notice in 14-point boldface type or capital letters: "IMPORTANT NOTICE: IF YOUR SEPARATE INTEREST IS PLACED IN FORECLOSURE BECAUSE YOU ARE BEHIND IN YOUR ASSESSMENTS, IT MAY BE SOLD WITHOUT COURT ACTION." Under § 5660(b), the notice must include "an itemized statement of the charges owed by the owner," broken out among delinquent assessments, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, late charges, and interest. Under § 5660(e), the owner has "the right to dispute the assessment debt by submitting a written request for dispute resolution to the association pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program," and under § 5660(f), "the right to request alternative dispute resolution with a neutral third party ... before the association may initiate foreclosure against the owner's separate interest, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." Separately, Civil Code § 5670 restates the dispute-resolution offer in more general terms: "Prior to recording a lien for delinquent assessments, an association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program."

HOW THE LIEN IS ACTUALLY CREATED AND ITS PRIORITY
The debt described in Civil Code § 5650 becomes an actual, recorded lien on an owner's separate interest only when the association takes an additional statutory step. Civil Code § 5675(a) provides: "The amount of the assessment, plus any costs of collection, late charges, and interest assessed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, shall be a lien on the owner's separate interest in the common interest development from and after the time the association causes to be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the separate interest is located, a notice of delinquent assessment, which shall state the amount of the assessment and other sums imposed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, a legal description of the owner's separate interest in the common interest development against which the assessment and other sums are levied, and the name of the record owner of the separate interest in the common interest development against which the lien is imposed." If the lien is to be enforced by nonjudicial foreclosure, Section 5675(c) further requires that "the notice of delinquent assessment shall state the name and address of the trustee authorized by the association to enforce the lien by sale." Once recorded, Civil Code § 5680 provides that the resulting lien "shall be prior to all other liens recorded subsequent to the notice of delinquent assessment, except that the declaration may provide for the subordination thereof to any other liens and encumbrances." If a notice of delinquent assessment affecting 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: May 15, 2026.

FINES AND PENALTIES CANNOT BE ENFORCED THROUGH THE ASSESSMENT LIEN
California law limits an association's ability to use its lien and foreclosure remedies to collect fines and penalties, as distinct from assessments themselves. This limitation applies to any assessment lien Meadowbrook Homeowners Association may record or seek to foreclose against 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. Civil Code § 5725(a) permits one narrow exception: "A monetary charge imposed by the association as a means of reimbursing the association for costs incurred by the association in the repair of damage to common area and facilities caused by a member or the member's guest or tenant may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c, provided the authority to impose a lien is set forth in the governing documents." Outside that exception, Civil Code § 5725(b) is explicit: "A monetary penalty imposed by the association as a disciplinary measure for failure of a member to comply with the governing documents, except for the late payments, may not be characterized nor treated in the governing documents as an assessment that may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c." The statutory notice required in an association's annual policy statement, Civil Code § 5730, restates the same limitation for owners: "The association may not use nonjudicial foreclosure to collect fines or penalties, except for costs to repair common area damaged by a member or a member's guests, if the governing documents provide for this."

MINIMUM DOLLAR AMOUNT AND DELINQUENCY PERIOD BEFORE FORECLOSURE
California law sets a minimum dollar amount and, alternatively, a minimum delinquency period before an association may use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure to collect delinquent assessments. Civil Code § 5720(b) provides that an association seeking to collect "delinquent regular or special assessments of an amount less than one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800), not including any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, or interest, may not collect that debt through judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure," though it may still pursue small claims court, or record a lien it may not yet foreclose. Section 5720(b)(2) provides that an association that records a lien in this situation "may not foreclose until the amount of the delinquent assessments secured by the lien ... equals or exceeds one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800) or the assessments secured by the lien are more than 12 months delinquent." Section 5720(c) confirms that "[t]he limitation on foreclosure of assessment liens for amounts under the stated minimum in this section does not apply to" assessments "more than 12 months delinquent," assessments on time-share estates, or assessments owed by the developer. If a total delinquent-assessment amount for Pat T. Alvarez's account with Meadowbrook Homeowners Association has been stated, it is stated as: $2,450.00.

BOARD VOTES REQUIRED TO RECORD A LIEN AND TO INITIATE FORECLOSURE
California law requires the association's board itself — not staff or an outside collection agent — to make two separate decisions in this process, each by a specified vote recorded in the board's minutes, and requires a further dispute-resolution offer before the second decision. These requirements apply to any decision by Meadowbrook Homeowners Association's board to record a lien against, or foreclose upon, 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. First, before a lien for delinquent assessments is recorded, Civil Code § 5673 provides: "For liens recorded on or after January 1, 2006, the decision to record a lien for delinquent assessments shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an open meeting. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of that meeting." Second, before the association initiates foreclosure of a lien that has already been validly recorded, Civil Code § 5705(b) requires the association to first offer dispute resolution: "the association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program ... or alternative dispute resolution ... The decision to pursue dispute resolution or a particular type of alternative dispute resolution shall be the choice of the owner, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." The decision to actually initiate foreclosure is then governed by § 5705(c): "The decision to initiate foreclosure of a lien for delinquent assessments that has been validly recorded shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an executive session. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of the next meeting of the board open to all members. The board shall maintain the confidentiality of the owner or owners of the separate interest by identifying the matter in the minutes by the parcel number of the property, rather than the name of the owner or owners. A board vote to approve foreclosure of a lien shall take place at least 30 days prior to any public sale."

WAITING PERIOD, TRUSTEE'S SALE MECHANICS, AND THE RIGHT OF REDEMPTION
Once a lien has been recorded and the association has completed the steps described above, California law sets further mechanics and timing for an actual sale of 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. Civil Code § 5700(a) provides that, subject to other provisions of the article, "after the expiration of 30 days following the recording of a lien created pursuant to Section 5675, the lien may be enforced in any manner permitted by law, including sale by the court, sale by the trustee designated in the notice of delinquent assessment, or sale by a trustee substituted pursuant to Section 2934a." If a trustee's sale is used, Civil Code § 5710(a) requires that it "be conducted in accordance with Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c applicable to the exercise of powers of sale in mortgages and deeds of trust" — the same statutory notice-of-default and notice-of-sale framework used for mortgage foreclosures. Section 5710(b) adds an association-specific requirement on top of that framework: "the association shall serve a notice of default on the person named as the owner of the separate interest in the association's records or, if that person has designated a legal representative ..., on that legal representative," served "in accordance with the manner of service of summons" under the Code of Civil Procedure. Unlike a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure sale, a completed HOA assessment-lien foreclosure sale carries a statutory right of redemption: Civil Code § 5715(b) provides that "[a] nonjudicial foreclosure by an association to collect upon a debt for delinquent assessments shall be subject to a right of redemption[, and t]he redemption period within which the separate interest may be redeemed from a foreclosure sale under this paragraph ends 90 days after the sale."

Under California Civil Code § 5650(a), "[a] regular or special assessment and any late charges, reasonable fees and costs of collection, reasonable attorney’s fees, if any, and interest, if any, as determined in accordance with subdivision (b), shall be a debt of the owner of the separate interest at the time the assessment or other sums are levied." Section 5650(b) fixes when that debt becomes delinquent and what may then be added to it: regular and special assessments are "delinquent 15 days after they become due, unless the declaration provides a longer time period," and once delinquent the association may recover reasonable costs of collection (including reasonable attorney's fees), "a late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars ($10), whichever is greater" (unless the declaration sets a smaller amount), and interest "at an annual interest rate not to exceed 12 percent, commencing 30 days after the assessment becomes due" (unless the declaration sets a lower rate). If a dollar figure has been stated as delinquent on Pat T. Alvarez's account with Meadowbrook Homeowners Association, it is stated as: $2,450.00, as of March 1, 2026.

expectedJSON.body: Before recording a lien for delinquent assessments against 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA to collect a debt owed by Pat T. Alvarez, California law requires the association to give written notice and certain rights. Civil Code § 5660 provides: "At least 30 days prior to recording a lien upon the separate interest of the owner of record to collect a debt that is past due under Section 5650, the association shall notify the owner of record in writing by certified mail" of a specified list of items. Under § 5660(a), those items include "a general description of the collection and lien enforcement procedures of the association," the owner's right to inspect association records, and a required notice in 14-point boldface type or capital letters: "IMPORTANT NOTICE: IF YOUR SEPARATE INTEREST IS PLACED IN FORECLOSURE BECAUSE YOU ARE BEHIND IN YOUR ASSESSMENTS, IT MAY BE SOLD WITHOUT COURT ACTION." Under § 5660(b), the notice must include "an itemized statement of the charges owed by the owner," broken out among delinquent assessments, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, late charges, and interest. Under § 5660(e), the owner has "the right to dispute the assessment debt by submitting a written request for dispute resolution to the association pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program," and under § 5660(f), "the right to request alternative dispute resolution with a neutral third party ... before the association may initiate foreclosure against the owner's separate interest, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." Separately, Civil Code § 5670 restates the dispute-resolution offer in more general terms: "Prior to recording a lien for delinquent assessments, an association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program."

expectedJSON.body: California law limits an association's ability to use its lien and foreclosure remedies to collect fines and penalties, as distinct from assessments themselves. This limitation applies to any assessment lien Meadowbrook Homeowners Association may record or seek to foreclose against 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. Civil Code § 5725(a) permits one narrow exception: "A monetary charge imposed by the association as a means of reimbursing the association for costs incurred by the association in the repair of damage to common area and facilities caused by a member or the member's guest or tenant may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c, provided the authority to impose a lien is set forth in the governing documents." Outside that exception, Civil Code § 5725(b) is explicit: "A monetary penalty imposed by the association as a disciplinary measure for failure of a member to comply with the governing documents, except for the late payments, may not be characterized nor treated in the governing documents as an assessment that may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c." The statutory notice required in an association's annual policy statement, Civil Code § 5730, restates the same limitation for owners: "The association may not use nonjudicial foreclosure to collect fines or penalties, except for costs to repair common area damaged by a member or a member's guests, if the governing documents provide for this."

expectedJSON.body: California law sets a minimum dollar amount and, alternatively, a minimum delinquency period before an association may use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure to collect delinquent assessments. Civil Code § 5720(b) provides that an association seeking to collect "delinquent regular or special assessments of an amount less than one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800), not including any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, or interest, may not collect that debt through judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure," though it may still pursue small claims court, or record a lien it may not yet foreclose. Section 5720(b)(2) provides that an association that records a lien in this situation "may not foreclose until the amount of the delinquent assessments secured by the lien ... equals or exceeds one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800) or the assessments secured by the lien are more than 12 months delinquent." Section 5720(c) confirms that "[t]he limitation on foreclosure of assessment liens for amounts under the stated minimum in this section does not apply to" assessments "more than 12 months delinquent," assessments on time-share estates, or assessments owed by the developer. If a total delinquent-assessment amount for Pat T. Alvarez's account with Meadowbrook Homeowners Association has been stated, it is stated as: $2,450.00.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires the association's board itself — not staff or an outside collection agent — to make two separate decisions in this process, each by a specified vote recorded in the board's minutes, and requires a further dispute-resolution offer before the second decision. These requirements apply to any decision by Meadowbrook Homeowners Association's board to record a lien against, or foreclose upon, 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. First, before a lien for delinquent assessments is recorded, Civil Code § 5673 provides: "For liens recorded on or after January 1, 2006, the decision to record a lien for delinquent assessments shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an open meeting. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of that meeting." Second, before the association initiates foreclosure of a lien that has already been validly recorded, Civil Code § 5705(b) requires the association to first offer dispute resolution: "the association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program ... or alternative dispute resolution ... The decision to pursue dispute resolution or a particular type of alternative dispute resolution shall be the choice of the owner, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." The decision to actually initiate foreclosure is then governed by § 5705(c): "The decision to initiate foreclosure of a lien for delinquent assessments that has been validly recorded shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an executive session. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of the next meeting of the board open to all members. The board shall maintain the confidentiality of the owner or owners of the separate interest by identifying the matter in the minutes by the parcel number of the property, rather than the name of the owner or owners. A board vote to approve foreclosure of a lien shall take place at least 30 days prior to any public sale."

expectedJSON.body: Once a lien has been recorded and the association has completed the steps described above, California law sets further mechanics and timing for an actual sale of 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA. Civil Code § 5700(a) provides that, subject to other provisions of the article, "after the expiration of 30 days following the recording of a lien created pursuant to Section 5675, the lien may be enforced in any manner permitted by law, including sale by the court, sale by the trustee designated in the notice of delinquent assessment, or sale by a trustee substituted pursuant to Section 2934a." If a trustee's sale is used, Civil Code § 5710(a) requires that it "be conducted in accordance with Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c applicable to the exercise of powers of sale in mortgages and deeds of trust" — the same statutory notice-of-default and notice-of-sale framework used for mortgage foreclosures. Section 5710(b) adds an association-specific requirement on top of that framework: "the association shall serve a notice of default on the person named as the owner of the separate interest in the association's records or, if that person has designated a legal representative ..., on that legal representative," served "in accordance with the manner of service of summons" under the Code of Civil Procedure. Unlike a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure sale, a completed HOA assessment-lien foreclosure sale carries a statutory right of redemption: Civil Code § 5715(b) provides that "[a] nonjudicial foreclosure by an association to collect upon a debt for delinquent assessments shall be subject to a right of redemption[, and t]he redemption period within which the separate interest may be redeemed from a foreclosure sale under this paragraph ends 90 days after the sale."
